# Correlating Cumulative Series

Two running totals correlate strongly with each other almost regardless of what they
count. The statistic is measuring **time**, not a relationship — and it is one of the few
analytical errors that reliably produces a *better*-looking result than doing it correctly.

## Why it happens

A cumulative series is monotone non-decreasing by construction. Every pair of monotone
series is therefore close to a monotone function of a common index, and Pearson's *r* over
them approaches 1 whether or not the underlying daily quantities have anything to do with
each other. Cumulative national coffee sales correlate with cumulative reported cases of
anything, in any country, over any period.

The daily series that generated them may be uncorrelated, negatively correlated, or
correlated at a lag. None of that survives the cumulation.

## How it hides

The failure has no symptom. There is no error, no warning, and no diagnostic that fires —
the output is a high correlation coefficient, which is the result the analyst was hoping
for. In the coursework version this concept was written from, cumulative case counts were
used directly as a predictor and the notebook ended with a causal-sounding conclusion. It
looked like the strongest finding in the document.

The neighbouring version of the same mistake is a **lag expressed in row offsets**. Row
`n-2` is "two days ago" only if the series has no gaps; one missing day silently shifts
every lag in the dataset. Lags belong on calendar dates.

## The correction

**Difference before analysing.** New cases per day, not cases to date. Then normalise by
population, so that area size is not doing the work — cumulative *and* un-normalised is the
combination that measures nothing but how big and how old each area is.

`validation.py` enforces the precondition that makes differencing meaningful: the input
must be a complete daily series per area with no gaps and no decreases. A cumulative count
that goes *down* is a revision, and revisions have to be handled deliberately rather than
differenced into negative "new cases".

Report both pooled and within-area correlations. The gap between them is where the
ecological fallacy lives: a pooled statistic can be dominated entirely by differences
*between* areas while the within-area relationship is flat or reversed.

## What is left even when it is done right

An area-day correlation is still a **descriptive ecological screen**. It cannot support an
individual-level or causal claim, because seasonality, policy, mobility, weather, testing
access, reporting delay and demographics are all unmodelled and all plausible. The honest
output names them. See [[reproducible-analysis]] for the other half — a result nobody can
regenerate cannot be checked for this either.
